concept_card.statement: For small swings, a pendulum's period T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g, not amplitude or bob mass.
concept_card.analogy: A bigger swing is a longer lap run faster, so lap time stays the same.
steps: Divide by m: acceleration = -(g/L)x, mass cancels
So T = 2π√(L/g): no amplitude, no mass
concept_card.worked_example: L = 1.0 m, g = π² m/s²: T = 2π√(1/π²) = 2.0 s, for a 3° or 6° swing, light or heavy bob.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If I pull it further, it has more distance to cover, so one swing takes longer.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Walking a longer distance normally takes more time.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Pulling further also gives a bigger restoring force, so the bob moves faster. For small angles the extra speed exactly makes up for the extra distance.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: For small swings, the period does not depend on amplitude.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: The bigger swing goes faster at the bottom, so it finishes first.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: You can see the wide-swinging bob whizzing past faster.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: It is faster, but it also has a longer path. For small angles speed and distance both scale with amplitude, so the time per swing stays the same.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Bigger and smaller small swings take exactly the same time per oscillation.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: A heavier bob changes the period, it swings faster or slower than a light one.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Heavy things feel harder to move, and for a spring a heavier mass really does slow it (T = 2π√(m/k)).
remediation_cards.why_wrong: In a pendulum gravity supplies the restoring force, and it grows with mass. More pull and more inertia cancel, like all objects falling together.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: A simple pendulum's period depends on L and g only, not on bob mass.

contrast_probes.probe: If you pull the same pendulum further out before letting go, does each swing take more time or less time?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: More time, because it has a longer path to cover.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Less time, because it moves faster.

contrast_probes.probe: Two pendulums of the same length are released from the same small angle, one with a light bob and one with a heavy bob; would they stay in step?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, they start from the same angle so they cover the same distance and stay together.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, the heavy one will swing at a different speed and drift apart.

contrast_probes.probe: What would you change to make a pendulum come back sooner: release it from higher up, or hang a heavier bob?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Release it from higher up so it goes faster.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Hang a heavier bob, since mass changes the swing time.

contrast_probes.probe: A pendulum takes 2 s per swing at 4°; roughly how long does it take at 8°, still a small angle?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: More than 2 s, maybe about 4 s, because it goes twice as far.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Still 2 s, because the time doesn't depend on how wide it swings.

contrast_probes.probe: A bob released from 10° moves faster at the bottom than one released from 5°; does that mean it finishes its swing first?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, faster means it gets back first.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it also has farther to go, so both take the same time.

contrast_probes.probe: If you replace a 100 g bob with a 400 g bob on the same string, what happens to the period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It changes, the heavier bob swings at a different rate.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same, because mass cancels and only L and g matter.

verify_flags: Amplitude independence holds only for small angles (sinθ ≈ θ); exact period grows slightly at large angles.
O3-R contrasts with spring-mass T = 2π√(m/k), where mass does matter.
